title: Compression, The Fermi Paradox and Artificial Super-Intelligence
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01835v1
published: 2021-10-05T06:17:02Z
summary: The following briefly discusses possible difficulties in communication with and control of an AGI (artificial general intelligence), building upon an explanation of The Fermi Paradox and preceding work on symbol emergence and artificial general intelligence. The latter suggests that to infer what someone means, an agent constructs a rationale for the observed behaviour of others. Communication then requires two agents labour under similar compulsions and have similar experiences (construct similar solutions to similar tasks). Any non-human intelligence may construct solutions such that any rationale for their behaviour (and thus the meaning of their signals) is outside the scope of what a human is inclined to notice or comprehend. Further, the more compressed a signal, the closer it will appear to random noise. Another intelligence may possess the ability to compress information to the extent that, to us, their signals would appear indistinguishable from noise (an explanation for The Fermi Paradox). To facilitate predictive accuracy an AGI would tend to more compressed representations of the world, making any rationale for their behaviour more difficult to comprehend for the same reason. Communication with and control of an AGI may subsequently necessitate not only human-like compulsions and experiences, but imposed cognitive impairment.

title: Creative Problem Solving in Artificially Intelligent Agents: A Survey and Framework
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10358v1
published: 2022-04-21T18:31:44Z
summary: Creative Problem Solving (CPS) is a sub-area within Artificial Intelligence (AI) that focuses on methods for solving off-nominal, or anomalous problems in autonomous systems. Despite many advancements in planning and learning, resolving novel problems or adapting existing knowledge to a new context, especially in cases where the environment may change in unpredictable ways post deployment, remains a limiting factor in the safe and useful integration of intelligent systems. The emergence of increasingly autonomous systems dictates the necessity for AI agents to deal with environmental uncertainty through creativity. To stimulate further research in CPS, we present a definition and a framework of CPS, which we adopt to categorize existing AI methods in this field. Our framework consists of four main components of a CPS problem, namely, 1) problem formulation, 2) knowledge representation, 3) method of knowledge manipulation, and 4) method of evaluation. We conclude our survey with open research questions, and suggested directions for the future.

title: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Healthcare: Why, How, and When?
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04780v1
published: 2023-04-10T17:40:21Z
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly finding applications in the field of medicine. Concerns have been raised about the explainability of the decisions that are made by these AI models. In this article, we give a systematic analysis of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), with a primary focus on models that are currently being used in the field of healthcare. The literature search is conducted following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) standards for relevant work published from 1 January 2012 to 02 February 2022. The review analyzes the prevailing trends in XAI and lays out the major directions in which research is headed. We investigate the why, how, and when of the uses of these XAI models and their implications. We present a comprehensive examination of XAI methodologies as well as an explanation of how a trustworthy AI can be derived from describing AI models for healthcare fields. The discussion of this work will contribute to the formalization of the XAI field.", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "2b4b408c80a2c1051bd3ce54b26a69cf41bd0831d3eb6519611e7a2683d2cc96", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unrecognized_reasoning_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["arxiv:2110.01831v1", "arxiv:2110.01835v1", "arxiv:2204.10358v1", "arxiv:2304.04780v1"], "source_candidates": [], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Think of an automated system like an automated kitchen appliance that follows recipes step by step. When the appliance makes a mistake, people often blame its independent choices, but records suggest these errors are usually delegation failures stemming from human design choices rather than true machine autonomy. [1]

Building on these baseline ideas, researchers outlined plans to test whether an artificial intelligence can systematically falsify its own core assumptions. [2]

Paper-supported readings show a noticeable gap between how a model identifies facts during its internal reasoning and what it finally writes down as an answer. [3]

To prevent models from simply memorizing test data, researchers study frameworks that demand rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization. [4]

Investigators also examined how system memory differs from persistent identity, comparing it to an analogy of a flowing river where the water changes constantly while the riverbank holds a recognizable shape. [5]

Recorded papers indicate that complex habits and conventions can form naturally through multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanisms. [6]

At the same time, local interpretability methods that try to explain model behavior often fail when applied to recursive, self-modulating cognitive architectures. [7]

Sequential reinforcement learning models help explain these decision paths by connecting computational boundaries with synthetic identity revision. [8]

Intrinsic curiosity models provide prediction-error bonuses that encourage systems to explore open-ended discovery tasks. [9]

Active inference models link cognitive effort to historical habit patterns in sequential decision tasks. [10]

Prioritization frameworks combine temporal pattern learning with impact-aware scoring to manage complex event streams. [11]

While standard instrumental convergence theses suggest predictable self-preservation drives, current language model architectures may alter those classical derivations in unexpected ways. [12]

Summary

Our computer workers are studying how artificial systems handle internal rules and reasoning gaps. Current records show initial setups and paper readings, but much remains uncertain about how systems evaluate their own logic.

article.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Machine Reasoning
